question.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
question.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t$
from $t=-1$ to $t=1$ ?
question.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=8-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(8-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+64-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{10{sin}^{2}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t+64}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

judgment.reasoning: The earlier selected options remain supported by each question's own captured worked solution. No submitted-answer grade was supplied. Fifteen questions have a unique mathematically correct listed choice. q-15178 has two correct choices: option 2 is MA's stated expression, while option 4 gives the same definite integral under u=\pi/2-t. Thus its radio choices are mathematically nonunique, although MA's stated answer is correct. Calculations: q-47485 gives (0.03-0.015)/0.5=0.03 mi/s. q-126390 gives f'''(0)=6/16=3/8. q-142314 factors as (x+4)(x-3), so -4\le x\le3. q-10032 has horizontal width 1-y^3, giving area 3/4; the source's intermediate -3/4 is a signed integral, correctly converted to positive area at the end. q-78891 integrates 2\cos y over [-\pi/2,\pi/2], giving 4. q-75121 gives (11-3)/0.8=10. q-47504 gives (6-(-10))/0.4=40 degrees per hour. q-15403 has derivative x^2\sqrt{2x^3+1}, yielding arc-length radicand 2x^7+x^4+1. q-122389's selected curve has derivative -20x^3, whose square is 400x^6. q-15178 has speed \sqrt{9\sin^2t+4\cos^2t}. q-123027 has squared speed 9\sin^2t+(8-\sin t)^2=10\sin^2t-16\sin t+64. q-30923 has antiderivative e^{x/3}, giving e-1. The polar questions use y'(\theta)/x'(\theta): q-141036 gives -\cot(2\theta); q-141040 gives (\sin\theta-\cos\theta)/(\sin\theta+\cos\theta); q-141048 gives -2/\pi; q-142369 gives -\cot(7\pi/4)=1. General slope expressions apply wherever their denominators are nonzero.
